findings.claim: Thomas Malthus is called "A Victorian economist (1766-1834)" in the <dfn> definition and the glossary.
findings.truth: Malthus died on 23 December 1834; Victoria came to the throne in June 1837, so he was never a Victorian. The definition prints the dates that contradict it, and Lesson 8 already calls him simply "an economist".
findings.evidence: Dates given in the definition itself; L8 glossary "Thomas Malthus": "Thomas Robert Malthus (1766-1834), an economist".

findings.claim: "He presented wealthy society as 'pleasant, ordered and extravagant' and contrasted it with poor society shown as 'disordered, barbaric and unhappy.'"
findings.truth: Neither phrase is in the novella. The quotation marks in a sentence beginning "He presented" invite a student to quote them as Dickens's words in an AO2 answer. Quotation marks removed; the point is kept as the lesson's own summary.
findings.evidence: Grep of the Gutenberg text (#46) for "extravagant" returns only Stave 3, "most extravagant contortions"; "barbaric" returns nothing.

findings.claim: Flashcard 1: answer "blacking factory", prompt "A factory where workers pasted labels onto pots of boot blacking, a type of shoe polish."
findings.truth: The prompt prints both words of its own answer, so the card tests nothing. Prompt reworded; the glossary definition is left intact.

findings.claim: Flashcards 4 and 5 are cloze fragments: answer "Charles" for "_____ Dickens published A Christmas Carol...", answer "1843" for "In _____ Dickens read a Parliamentary Commission report...".
findings.truth: Single-word cloze answers on sentence fragments. Card 4 tested the author's first name. Both rebuilt as questions; card 4 now asks which economist Scrooge echoes (answer Thomas Malthus), card 5 keeps the answer 1843.

findings.claim: Fred's greeting is quoted as "Merry Christmas, uncle! God save you!"
findings.truth: The text reads "A merry Christmas, uncle! God save you!" The dropped article and the capital M matter because this is the line students memorise.

findings.claim: "Darkness was cheap, and Scrooge liked it" in L2 content, L2 practice question 6, L2 knowledge check 5 (matching item), L3 practice question 1 mark scheme, L4 content, L8 content and L8 knowledge check 4.
findings.truth: Dickens writes it in the present tense: "Darkness is cheap, and Scrooge liked it." Seven places across four lessons carry the wrong wording, including a matching item and a fill-the-gap stem.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave I, line 590: "Up Scrooge went, not caring a button for that. Darkness is cheap, and Scrooge liked it."

findings.claim: Marley "cries ... 'I cannot rest, I cannot stay, I cannot linger anywhere. No rest, no peace. Incessant torture of remorse.'"
findings.truth: Two separate speeches, pages apart, welded into one quotation. "No rest, no peace. Incessant torture of remorse." is Marley's answer to Scrooge's "Seven years dead... And travelling all the time!", well after the "I cannot rest" speech.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave I, lines 832-833 and lines 853-855.

findings.claim: The <dfn> definition, glossary entry and flashcard for "knowledge" read "The state of being aware of and able to think and perceive".
findings.truth: That is the dictionary definition of consciousness, not of knowledge. Replaced with "Facts and understanding gained through learning"; the lesson-specific second half is kept.

findings.claim: Printed extract: "'Another idol has displaced me,' said a fair young woman in a changed voice, 'a golden one.'"
findings.truth: The speech tag is invented. Dickens writes "a fair young girl in a mourning-dress", never "in a changed voice", and "A golden one" is Belle's reply to Scrooge's question "What Idol has displaced you?", not part of the same speech. The extract is replaced with the verbatim exchange.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave II, lines 1603-1616; grep for "changed voice" returns nothing.

findings.claim: "the weakness of the fire echoes the 'small fire' he allows Bob Cratchit in Stave 1".
findings.truth: "A very small fire" is Scrooge's own fire. The clerk's fire "was so very much smaller that it looked like one coal". The quotation is attached to the wrong character.

findings.claim: "the Ghost replies using Scrooge's own words: 'If these shadows remain unaltered by the future... the child will die.'"
findings.truth: That line is the Spirit's own wording. Scrooge's words are turned on him a few lines later ("he had better do it, and decrease the surplus population") and again at the end of the stave ("Are there no prisons?"). The lesson's own next section says so, so it contradicts itself. Dickens also capitalises "Future".

findings.claim: "no one said or thought it was a small pudding for a large family", printed the same way as the extract for practice question 2.
findings.truth: Dickens writes "nobody said or thought it was at all a small pudding for a large family". The extract a student is told to analyse is misquoted.

findings.claim: "Ignorance" is defined, in the <dfn> and the glossary, as "the allegorical children hidden beneath the Ghost of Christmas Present's robe".
findings.truth: Ignorance is the boy; Want is the girl. The definition describes both children and so contradicts the sentence it sits inside ("The Ghost identifies the boy as Ignorance and the girl as Want").
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave III, line 2793: "This boy is Ignorance. This girl is Want."

findings.claim: "remember there is no separate SPaG mark on Paper 1 Section B".
findings.truth: The fact is right but the wording is a banned paper-and-section code in a student-facing field, which the house validator rejects for the whole unit. Rewritten as "the 19th-century novel question".
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT.md banned strings; spec Paper 1 carries AO4 at 2.5% on the Shakespeare question only.

findings.claim: "Dickens writes that Bob had carried Tiny Tim on his shoulders and 'walked very fast indeed' - suggesting the unbearable weight of grief."
findings.truth: The line is Mrs Cratchit's, not the narrator's, and it remembers how Bob walked BEFORE Tim died, when the boy "was very light to carry". Dickens's grief signal is the opposite: Peter says his father "has walked a little slower than he used, these few last evenings". The lesson reverses the meaning of the evidence.

findings.claim: "The use of the word 'Phantom' rather than 'Ghost' or 'Spirit' suggests something more sinister", and knowledge check 1: "What word does Dickens use to describe the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come instead of 'Ghost' or 'Spirit'?" with options including Phantom and Spectre.
findings.truth: Dickens calls this ghost "this Spirit" in the second sentence of Stave 4 and "the Spirit" throughout, and Scrooge addresses it as "Spectre" and "Good Spirit". The premise is false, and the knowledge check has two defensible answers. Stem pinned to the opening line of Stave 4, where "Phantom" is uniquely right.

findings.claim: The thieves at Old Joe's "even stolen the buttons from his coat".
findings.truth: The undertaker's man sells "a seal or two, a pencil-case, a pair of sleeve-buttons, and a brooch of no great value". They are cufflinks taken from the dead man's room, not buttons cut off a coat.

findings.claim: The 30-mark band ladder in L5 Q5, L6 Q5, L7 Q5 and L8 Q5 prints "Top band" twice (26-30 and 16-20) and mixes "Upper band" with "Upper-mid band".
findings.truth: Six rows, six house band names. Relabelled Top / Upper-mid / Mid / Lower-mid / Low / Basic against the same mark ranges. The mark ranges themselves are correct for a 30-mark question.

findings.claim: "The emphasis on 'his own' - repeated three times in the opening lines".
findings.truth: It is repeated four times: the bedpost, the bed, the room and the Time.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave V: "YES! and the bedpost was his own. The bed was his own, the room was his own. Best and happiest of all, the Time before him was his own, to make amends in!"

findings.claim: The printed extract in practice question 3 reads "who did not die", while the same item's mark scheme rewards analysing "'Did NOT die' (Dickens's emphasis)".
findings.truth: Dickens emphasises NOT. The extract removes the very feature the mark scheme credits.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave V: "and to Tiny Tim, who did NOT die, he was a second father".

findings.claim: Mark scheme for question 3: "the repetition of 'good' (five times)".
findings.truth: The printed extract carries "good" four times: good a friend, good a master, good a man, good old city.

findings.claim: Flashcard 3: answer "cyclical structure", prompt "A narrative structure where the ending mirrors the beginning...".
findings.truth: The prompt contains the word "structure" from its own answer. Reworded to "A shape of storytelling where..."; the glossary definition is left intact.

findings.claim: Fred "declares: 'I say Merry Christmas and mean it!'"
findings.truth: Fabricated quotation. The phrase appears nowhere in the novella. Fred's real closing line in the counting house is "I'll keep my Christmas humour to the last. So A Merry Christmas, uncle!"
findings.evidence: Grep of Gutenberg #46 for "mean it" returns no hits; Stave I, lines 300-304.

findings.claim: Mark scheme for question 1: "The italicised emphasis (in the original text) shows Marley's anguish."
findings.truth: "Mankind was my business" carries no emphasis marking. This edition preserves Dickens's emphasis as capitals elsewhere ("did NOT die") and there is none here, so a student would be writing about something that is not on the exam paper. Replaced with Marley's cry of "Business!", which is in the text.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave I: "'Business!' cried the Ghost, wringing its hands again. 'Mankind was my business.'"

findings.claim: "Their Christmas dinner, where even the pudding is praised for its 'cheapness'".
findings.truth: It is the goose. "Its tenderness and flavour, size and cheapness, were the themes of universal admiration." Lesson 4 says goose, so the unit contradicts itself, and the pudding passage is the one about "a small pudding for a large family".

findings.claim: The Poor Law Amendment Act is defined, in the <dfn>, the glossary and a flashcard, as creating "workhouses as the only form of relief for the poor".
findings.truth: Outdoor relief continued after 1834 and was never abolished in many northern districts; the Act aimed to restrict it, not to remove it. Lesson 1 already says "the main form of relief", so the unit contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poor_Law_Amendment_Act_1834 - "Outdoor relief did continue after the PLAA was introduced"; "outdoor relief was never abolished in many Northern districts".

findings.claim: "Direct address: The narrator frequently addresses the reader directly ('Oh! But he was a tight-fisted hand at the grindstone, Scrooge!')."
findings.truth: That is an exclamation about Scrooge, not an address to the reader. Dickens does address the reader, so the technique label is fine but the example is wrong. Replaced with a real one.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #46, Stave I, lines 85-86: "You will therefore permit me to repeat, emphatically, that Marley was as dead as a door-nail."

findings.claim: Flashcards 4 and 5 are cloze fragments: answer "Dickens" for "_____ wrote the novella in 1843...", answer "Poor" for "The _____ Law Amendment Act of 1834 had created workhouses...".
findings.truth: "Poor" is a fragment of another card's answer in the same deck, and its prompt prints the rest of the Act's name. Both rebuilt as questions with the answers "Jacob Marley" and "Ignorance".

findings.claim: Flashcard 3: answer "Thomas Malthus", prompt "Thomas Robert Malthus (1766-1834), an economist who argued...".
findings.truth: The prompt prints the card's own answer. Prompt reworded to open with "An economist (1766-1834) who argued..."; the glossary entry keeps the full name.

findings.claim: Question 5 AO3 guidance: "the role of women (Belle has no choice but to release Scrooge from the engagement)".
findings.truth: Two defensible readings. The text shows Belle choosing: "I release you. With a full heart, for the love of him you once were." The contextual point that a Victorian woman had little power in a long engagement is fair, but "has no choice" contradicts the scene a student would quote. Either reword to "Belle releases Scrooge herself, though a Victorian woman had little power to hold him to it", or drop the parenthesis.

findings.claim: "Dickens establishes from the very first line that 'Marley was dead: to begin with' - a deliberate foreshadowing device."
findings.truth: Stating a fact at the start is not foreshadowing, and the lesson's own next sentence explains it correctly as establishing belief before the ghost appears. Only the label is loose; the quotation and the reasoning are right.

findings.claim: "Despite his poverty, Bob is cheerful and kind - 'he boasted no greatcoat' but still returned Fred's Christmas greetings 'cordially.'"
findings.truth: The text hyphenates "great-coat", and the phrase belongs to Bob leaving work at the end of Stave 1, not to the counting-house greeting. Both details are Stave 1 and both are about Bob, so no marks are at risk.

findings.claim: Unit-wide: the 4-, 8- and 12-mark ladders use "Upper band" and "Lower band" rather than the house ladder, and the mark ranges do not always match the label on the question type.
findings.truth: Recording only. This belongs with the corpus-wide band-ladder queue, not with 40 separate edits here. The four 30-mark ladders that printed "Top band" twice are fixed under F18.

findings.claim: "In 1800, only 60% of men and 40% of women were literate."
findings.truth: These are the usual signature-literacy estimates for England around 1800 and are widely repeated, so the figures stand, but they measure the ability to sign a marriage register rather than to read and write fluently.
findings.evidence: Standard signature-literacy series for England c.1800.

summary: Three HIGH findings: a banned paper-and-section code in the Lesson 5 exam tip, which the house validator rejects for the whole unit; a fabricated Fred quotation "I say Merry Christmas and mean it!" in Lesson 7; and Lesson 5 reading Mrs Cratchit's memory of Bob walking "very fast indeed" as the weight of grief, when it recalls the time before Tiny Tim died and Dickens's grief signal is that Bob now walks slower. Also a seven-place misquotation of "Darkness is cheap" across four lessons, an invented speech tag on a printed Belle extract, a Stave 3 line misattributed to Scrooge, the goose's cheapness given to the pudding, the 1834 Poor Law called the only form of relief, "knowledge" defined as consciousness, Malthus labelled Victorian though he died in 1834, and four 30-mark ladders that printed "Top band" twice. All 40 knowledge-check answer keys and all eight match orders are correct apart from one stem with two defensible answers (F16).
